metadata.title: Public Cloud Services Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how a public-cloud platform would need to change when a country requires locally controlled operations, customers gain a rapid right to leave, export controls remove scarce accelerators, or a regulated bank must exit a local operator while replacement AI capacity is constrained.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A customer creates a global cloud account, chooses a region and service, provisions resources through the provider control plane, stores data under provider-managed identity and encryption, consumes capacity, and pays metered charges. The design assumes the global provider remains the legal operator, APIs and exports remain available, and equivalent capacity can be purchased in an allowed region.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design separates customer organization, workload intent, legal operator, control plane, region, facility, support personnel, identity authority, key custodian, data and model copy, service contract, API representation, capacity entitlement, hardware class, export restriction, usage, billing, migration package, acceptance evidence, and deletion proof. A workload can change operator, service implementation, region, or capacity class without losing its security, sovereignty, economic, or portability obligations.
metadata.note: The tests attack control and dependency, not only availability. The explicit change is that a cloud service is no longer treated as one inseparable provider resource: operation, data custody, keys, capacity, interface, commercial rights, and exit evidence can each move under governed conditions.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: A government requires cloud operations, administrator access, and encryption-key control to remain under a local entity
stressors.detection: Final sovereignty law and licensing guidance, customer workload and data classifications, legal entities, regions and facilities, control-plane dependencies, support and administrator rosters, identity and key custody, telemetry paths, subcontractors, and audit requirements.
stressors.attractor: Data is physically in-country but provisioning, privileged support, identity recovery, key administration, telemetry, billing, and incident command still depend on global systems or personnel. Calling the region sovereign no longer satisfies customers or regulators, while a complete disconnected copy risks inconsistent security and operations.
stressors.businessReaction: Define the required control boundary, establish a licensed local operator, classify workloads, localize administrator and recovery authority, provide customer or local key custody, remove hidden cross-border dependencies, create bounded global support paths, test isolation and continuity, and provide current evidence to customers and regulators.
stressors.residue: Separate provider brand, legal operator, service contract, workload, data copy, control-plane function, administrative role, human operator, identity authority, key custodian, telemetry path, support action, subprocess, jurisdiction, policy, exception, and evidence. Sovereignty is evaluated per control and data path rather than assigned as one region label.

impacts.effect: Regulated customers can identify who operates every critical control and where authority, data, keys, and evidence reside.
Platform owners improve resilience while preserving explicit sovereignty over control, recovery, and support.
Provisioning verifies legal operator, admin path, identity recovery, key custody, telemetry, support, and isolation mode.
Audit-ready coverage requires evidence for each sovereign control path, not only an in-country resource address.
Adds sovereignty profiles, local operator controls, privileged-path inventory, key-custody choices, isolation tests, and evidence.
Carries sovereignty requirements from workload classification into runtime operations, support, recovery, and audit.
Evaluates every resource and control path against jurisdiction, operator, data, support, and exception policy.
Separates key ownership, custody, use, recovery, rotation, revocation, and legal operator.
Scopes human and service authority to locally governed identities, roles, sessions, resources, and emergency paths.
Owns sovereignty with local operations, legal, identity, key, support, service, audit, and customer teams.
Makes control-path sovereignty, not just regional hosting, a public-cloud benchmark.

stressors.name: A cloud-portability law gives customers thirty days to leave with data, configuration, identity, and audit history
stressors.detection: Final portability law and contract terms, customer termination or migration request, workload and dependency inventory, service APIs and schemas, data volume and formats, identity and key state, logs and evidence, marketplace licenses, egress charges, deletion requirements, and target-provider acceptance tests.
stressors.attractor: Downloading primary data is not enough to recreate managed databases, events, identities, policies, keys, network rules, service configuration, operational history, or licensed dependencies. A provider-specific export can be technically complete but unusable elsewhere, while the original environment continues creating data and charges during migration.
stressors.businessReaction: Agree the exit scope and cutover, inventory dependencies, generate documented portable packages, preserve incremental changes, provide target validation, migrate identity and keys safely, resolve marketplace rights, cap or waive exit costs as required, prove handoff, retain legally required evidence, and delete remaining copies.
stressors.residue: Separate workload intent, provider resource, open representation, data snapshot, change log, configuration, identity mapping, key transfer or re-encryption, network policy, operational evidence, third-party license, migration wave, acceptance test, cutover, customer sign-off, retained record, deletion task, and deletion proof. Exit is a lifecycle with verifiable outcomes, not one archive file.

impacts.effect: Enterprise cloud adoption remains governable because every material workload has a tested and economically clear exit path.
Cloud leaders can operate a portfolio with explicit portability, dependency, contract, and deletion readiness.
Portfolio operation tracks exit completeness, format fitness, target validation, change capture, cost, and deletion evidence.
Time to first production workload includes successful reconstruction from documented portable artifacts.
Adds workload dependency inventory, portable export contracts, target tests, migration controls, commercial closure, and deletion proof.
Treats migration into, between, and out of cloud as the same governed workload transition capability.
Plans snapshots, deltas, transformations, rehearsals, cutover, validation, rollback, and source closure.
Provides durable versioned packages, manifests, checksums, lifecycle controls, and verified transfer.
Publishes machine- and human-readable schemas, semantics, limitations, reconstruction steps, and compatibility changes.
Owns exit readiness with service teams, identity, key, networking, marketplace, billing, legal, support, and target providers.
Makes demonstrable hybrid and cross-provider workload portability a cloud-adoption benchmark.

stressors.name: Export controls and a supply shock make the planned accelerator class unavailable in several regions
stressors.detection: Government and supplier notices, customer and workload eligibility, region and facility inventory, accelerator model and origin, reservations and commitments, queued jobs, model and framework compatibility, energy constraints, service objectives, pricing, and marketplace alternatives.
stressors.attractor: AI training and inference designs assume one accelerator, managed service, region, and commercial commitment. Capacity already reserved may become illegal to deliver or physically unavailable; moving workloads can break model behavior, data residency, latency, cost, and software compatibility.
stressors.businessReaction: Classify affected customers and capacity, stop prohibited delivery, protect lawful commitments, compare eligible hardware and managed-model alternatives, adapt workloads, schedule scarce capacity by declared objectives, communicate performance and cost changes, refund unusable commitments, and diversify future supply.
stressors.residue: Separate workload objective, customer and beneficial user, jurisdictional eligibility, model and framework, required capability, accelerator type and origin, region, capacity pool, reservation, commitment, energy envelope, compatibility result, performance profile, price, allocation decision, alternative plan, and measured outcome. The workload binds to capabilities and constraints rather than one device SKU.

impacts.effect: Application builders can preserve an AI feature's purpose while hardware, region, service, latency, and economics change.
Teams add data and AI capabilities through portable workload requirements and measured alternatives.
Control compares eligible capacity, model behavior, data location, latency, energy, price, commitment, and fallback.
Cost anomaly response includes policy-driven capacity replacement and commitment correction, not only spend alerts.
Adds capability-based workload profiles, export eligibility, heterogeneous execution, migration tests, allocation, and outcome comparison.
Places capacity eligibility and substitute execution inside the normal AI build and operate path.
Catalogs accelerator capability, origin, region, energy, eligibility, inventory, reservation, and replacement options.
Versions models, runtimes, evaluations, deployment profiles, compatibility, routing, and fallback behavior.
Reconciles commitments, allocation policy, usage, substitute cost, refunds, budgets, and measured unit economics.
Owns workload continuity with accelerator, service, legal, capacity, FinOps, energy, migration, and customer teams.
Makes heterogeneous accelerator and managed-AI portability a cloud data-and-AI benchmark.

stressors.name: A regulated bank must leave a local cloud operator after its license is revoked while replacement accelerators are restricted
stressors.detection: Operator-license decision, workload and control-path inventory, bank classifications and deadlines, portable packages and deltas, keys and identities, accelerator eligibility and capacity, target regions and operators, compatibility tests, service and recovery objectives, commercial obligations, and deletion evidence.
stressors.attractor: The bank must remove workloads and data from an operator it can no longer use, but the obvious target cannot supply the same accelerators or accept global administration. Rebuilding from raw data would miss control evidence and service state; waiting for identical capacity violates the exit deadline.
stressors.businessReaction: Establish the regulatory perimeter, freeze unsafe changes, select an eligible operator and capability-based target, export versioned workload packages and deltas, transfer or re-encrypt keys, adapt AI execution, test controls and recovery, cut over in waves, settle commitments, and prove source deletion.
stressors.residue: No new structural change is required: sovereign control-path records select an eligible operator, portable workload packages reconstruct data, configuration, identity, and evidence, and capability-based accelerator profiles choose a lawful substitute. One migration case coordinates the existing transitions and proofs.

impacts.effect: Cloud operators can execute a regulated exit without losing security, observability, cost, or service accountability.
Platform teams preserve reliability and cost control through operator, region, service, and hardware change.
Recovery tracks export, delta, reconstruction, control tests, capacity substitution, cutover, rollback, cost, and deletion.
High-severity incident rate includes material failures introduced by regulated migration and substitute capacity.
Composes operator eligibility, migration evidence, target capacity, commercial closure, customer approval, and source deletion.
Reuses sovereignty, portability, and capacity residues to coordinate providers, commitments, migration, and financial treatment.
Restores workloads from portable protected state and validates recovery and service objectives at the target.
Resolves replacement service and license eligibility, contracts, entitlement, support, and commercial transfer.
Coordinates regulatory milestones, target readiness, workload exceptions, customer decisions, and evidence.
Coordinates the exit with sovereignty, migration, AI, capacity, security, finance, support, operator, and bank teams.
Makes controlled sovereign exit under scarce capacity a hyperscale-cloud resilience benchmark.
